utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume the hearing. Please be seated. Have the accused brought in, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, let me turn to you. I think I have forgotten my documents. Mr. Registrar, if you have the documents about the witness, you can give them to me. I think that we are beginning -- I am saying this for the public gallery because now we are in a public session -- we are going to begin the rebuttal, the general rebuttal; is that correct, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You asked us -- you know, I am absolutely obsessed with time, you know this by now -- you asked us and we gave you six days; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So the six days will begin right now. I don't know if you're going to actually need six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We will need considerably less time than six days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Could you tell us about how many days you need without really binding yourself to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm not bound, Mr. President, but approximately two days or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Two days or less. Very well. I'm not going to make any conclusions, Mr. Hayman, that we're going to take away two days from you. You asked for two days for your surrebuttal; is that correct? Will you need the two full days? Of course, I'm not going to take them away from you, realise that. Just because the Prosecutor has two days, you have to have two days too, but we might hope that you would use less than two days or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We may have none, Mr. President. We have to wait and hear what we are going to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that July is going to be devoted -- present us with enormous amounts of written documents. I feel that coming. But for the time being, we can begin with your rebuttal days, Mr. Prosecutor, and I think you are going to introduce a witness; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel. Our next witness will be Major Nicholas Short, and he is a British officer that served in the Gornji Vakuf area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We've got the summary, so you don't have to repeat it, and we will have the witness brought in. You're not asking for any particular protective measures, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, we are not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are going to tell the Tribunal your name, your given name, your rank in the army, because apparently you are a military man, your residence, if you like -- you don't have to do that -- and then you will take an oath, and after that, you will sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Major Nicholas Short, serving in the British army. I am currently stationed in Colchester.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you take the oath, please, according to the statement which is being handed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You may now be seated. Thank you for having come to the Tribunal. You have been called by the Prosecutor in the trial of General Blaskic who, at the time of the facts, was a Colonel. He is at your left. The Prosecutor called you, and he will begin by asking you a certain number of questions. After that, the Defence will ask you questions, and perhaps the Judges will have some as well. Mr. Registrar -- if there's nothing further to say, you can begin, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Major Short.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We speak the same language, so when I ask you a question in English, if you could pause just while the interpreters have time to translate the questions and then give us your answer, it will prevent the overlap or the merging of our questions and answers. So let me begin. Major Short, could you, first of all, tell the Judges about your background, and when you answer my questions, would you face to the Judges and direct your answers to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: I joined the army in 1983, and I am now a company commander serving with the 1st Battalion of the Royal Gloucester Barkshire and Wiltshire Regiment in Colchester. My rank is Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Major, could you tell us about your experiences when you went to Bosnia and Herzegovina, when you left Bosnia and Herzegovina, and what your duties and responsibilities were when you were in theatre?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: I deployed to Bosnia-Herzegovina in December of 1992, and I left there in June of 1993. On deployment, I was deployed as a military interpreter, having done a language course in England before I left. I was attached to "B" Company, 1 Cheshires, initially, who were in Gornji Vakuf, and I remained in Gornji Vakuf throughout my time, from November to June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you eventually become a liaison officer in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: Yes. When the fighting started in Gornji Vakuf, because of my rank and my military skills, in that I was able to command an armoured vehicle, I was used to move around the area in the role of a liaison officer, and also being able to speak the language, assisted in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you were a liaison officer from what date until approximately what date?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: I started my liaison duties, really, towards the end of January, round-about, I think about the 23rd of January, and I continued those duties through until the Prince of Wales Own Company arrived, and then I continued with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Major, I'd like to focus your attention on the conflict in Gornji Vakuf that erupted in January of 1993. Could you explain to the Judges those events?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: To the best of my memory, in early -- up until the 12th of January, 1993, there had been no fighting at all in the Gornji Vakuf area, although there was considerable tension due to the events in Prozor the year before. On the 12th, I was away up in Vitez taking a convoy up through to Sarajevo. On our return that evening, as we drove back into Gornji Vakuf, a large amount of small-arms fire was breaking out. As we drove back into the town, we were -- as the armoured vehicles moved back along the road, a group of HVO soldiers moved alongside us and then moved into positions where they could obviously engage the ARBiH forces. Subsequent to that, between the 12th and about the 17th, the conflict really was at a local level, small-arms fire, sporadic use of hand-held anti-armour weapons, and small mortar fire as well. During this time, there were a number of negotiations at a local level by UNPROFOR and the local commanders to attempt to resolve the problem. During this phase, the HVO commander of the area, Zrinko Tokic, informed us, UNPROFOR and the ARBiH, that if the problem was not resolved soon, then outside forces from Prozor and elsewhere would be brought in. On the 17th of January, an ultimatum was delivered to the ARBiH, and we were informed of the ultimatum, and the ultimatum -- I can't recall the details, but to the best of my knowledge, the sort of bottom line was that it called for the ARBiH forces to come under command of the HVO, to be suborned to the HVO. That ultimatum was delivered on the morning of the 17th, and it was not met by the evening of the 17th. On the morning of the 18th, I received a telephone call on the field telephone that we had to the HVO headquarters from Zrinko Tokic, who informed me that the HVO were about to attack Gornji Vakuf and that we should take cover in our prepared bunkers. Later, at about 0830, the attack started which involved the use of tanks and artillery and a mobile anti-aircraft cannon system. That fighting then went on for approximately six or seven days, and during that time, we could see quite considerable sort of fighting going on around the Gornji Vakuf area, not just restricted to the town. We could also see a number of villages burning and also we could see smoke from places that we couldn't physically see but we knew generally where they were. On about the 27th of January, we had been negotiating, and we reached some kind of an agreement, an agreement centred around a commission being formed in the UNPROFOR headquarters in Gornji Vakuf and a mobile team who would go out on the area and investigate various claims from one side or the other. This commission consisted of two Muslim police, military policemen from Bugojno and two Muslim -- sorry, two Bosnian Croat policemen from Bugojno, and myself and the ECMM. Over the following days, we then went out on the area and investigated various claims that had been made by one side or the other and reported back that evening. During that time, it became apparent to me that a number of villages had been burnt to the ground, and in one particular area had actually been blown up using military explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Major Short, I'm going to show you an exhibit, and you're familiar with this exhibit because last night you prepared this exhibit at my request, did you not?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While this exhibit is being marked and distributed, let me ask you two questions: You said while the fighting was going on from the 18th, approximately the 18th of January until the 27th of January, you could see the various villages burning.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you know the ethnic composition of those villages that you could observe, that you observed burning?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: At the time, we could only -- we knew roughly -- the ones we could see, yes, we knew what the ethnic composition was. The ones that we couldn't see, we didn't know at the time, but when I went round and found out, then it became apparent that all the villages that had been burned were Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Major, the court usher will be putting this map up on the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document 747.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Major Short, if you can explain to the Judges what this document represents?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: The map that is in front of you refers to -- the yellow highlighted groups of houses and villages refer to the villages that I went and visited over the course of about three or four days and discovered that all the houses in those villages had -- sorry, the vast majority of those houses in those villages had been burned and were uninhabitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were those all Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Major Short, you remained in Gornji Vakuf until June. To your knowledge, was anybody in the HVO disciplined or punished for burning Muslim houses in those villages?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Major, I want to direct your attention to another area, another topic, and that is a particular threat that occurred on the 5th of February, 1993. Could you please expand on that particular area of discussion?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: On the 5th of February, the fighting had been fairly low-key at that stage, it was sporadic small-arms fire. However, on the 5th, there was an eruption of heavier fighting. As a result of that, the HVO commander, Zrinko Tokic, rang up the headquarters, and informed us as well, that unless the fighting ceased, he would push two fuel tankers down from the hill above the Muslim part of town, the relay, as it was known, into the town and set fire to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Major, did you and UNPROFOR take that threat as a serious threat?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: Once we had seen the two fuel tankers on the hill then, yes, we did, and we had no choice other than to take it as a serious threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was the plan executed?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges why, in your opinion, it was not executed?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: In my opinion, one, that there was no fuel in the tankers, but we had to assume there was, but probably more likely was that on the day or the day subsequent to that, General Morillon visited, and there was a large press attendance there, and I believe Sky TV showed pictures of the two fuel tankers sitting above Gornji Vakuf, and I believe, in my opinion, that that is what prevented those being used in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me focus your attention on the conflict between the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats in the last week of January, the first week of February, 1993, in the Gornji Vakuf area. Did you see troops from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: To the best of my memory, in either the last week of January or the first week of February, I recall seeing, in the area of Karamustafic, which was an HVO checkpoint and had been used as a staging area, a band, a group of approximately 20 soldiers wearing HV uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did they have any marks of identification on them indicating they were from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: They were in combat, in camouflage uniforms, with -- obviously prepared for combat operations with their equipment, their weapons, and they had HV shoulder patches on their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How far away was this from Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: Off the top of my head, Karamustafic is about two to three kilometres south of Gornji Vakuf on the road between Gornji Vakuf and Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did it appear to you, Major Short, that these Croatian army troops were about to engage in combat against another force?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: I would -- I would say that they were in a known staging area and it was obvious that they were about to move forward. As to whether they were going to engage in combat, I was not in a position to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My last question, Major Short, is: When you and the various individuals who went around with you from the commission inspected the villages that are highlighted in yellow, could you give us your view on how these particular houses had been set afire?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: In all cases, the -- the area of Upper Hrasnica which had been destroyed using explosives, in all cases the villages had been burnt using some kind of flammable material setting fire to the buildings, and there was no indications that any combat had taken place in and around those buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Major Short, thank you very much. I have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to congratulate you, Mr. Harmon, for having fully respected and followed the summary that you submitted. I think that's very good. I would also like to thank the witness who was very concrete. We can now move to the Defence. The Defence wants to ask some questions as part of its surrebuttal -- its cross-examination, and please look at the Judges when you answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, could we move the ELMO slightly so that the witness and I can see each other?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I didn't mean to enlist the witness's labour on behalf of that mission, but I thank you, Major Short, and welcome to The Hague. My name is Russell Hayman and together with my colleague, Anto Nobilo, we represent General Blaskic. Have you met General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: I believe so, at a meeting once, in the Vitez area in which I was escorting some HVO officers up to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What kind of meeting was that?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: I believe -- well, the part of the meeting we were involved in was to negotiate the move of the Jajce Brigade, which was an ARBiH Brigade, up through there to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, this Jajce Brigade, it had been in the Gornji Vakuf area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: Yes, it had been in the Gornji Vakuf area since the fall of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So this was a brigade. Can you give us an estimate of how many ABiH soldiers were in this brigade?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: It would be difficult to say, but we estimated somewhere in the area between 500 and 600 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We need to pause between our question and answer, although I understand how the President felt when he had a native speaker in his own tongue. It's quite a pleasure to speak with you. Is it correct then that after the fall of Jajce, this brigade of some 500 to 600 BH army soldiers came to Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: They moved to an area about 12 kilometres to the southeast of Gornji Vakuf. The name of the village escapes me at the moment, but if I looked on a map, I would be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What had been the balance of forces in Gornji Vakuf prior to the arrival of this BiH brigade from Jajce?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that the introduction of this brigade resulted in a significant change in the balance of forces in the region?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: I would say that in terms of numbers of men, then possibly, yes. However, when we went to move the Jajce Brigade, they only had very limited small arms with them because they had lost them in the fall of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Putting aside the Jajce Brigade, how many BH army brigades were there in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was there even one brigade based in the town?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I know that there was both local defence forces had forces there, and I could only assume, because it was fairly early on in UNPROFOR's role there and we were not there to collect intelligence, we were there to escort humanitarian aid convoys. So we were focusing on that rather than on what units were located in the Gornji Vakuf area, but there was -- in answer to your original question, there was probably a parity of numbers, certainly what we would see on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: There was a balance of forces before the arrival of the Jajce Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: After the conflict erupted, you were told, on a number of occasions, that the arrival of this brigade from outside the area had destabilised relations between the HVO and the BH army in the region; correct?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: Yes. The HVO were very keen that the Jajce Brigade be moved because they felt that it had caused some problems within the area and obviously had worried people with 600 soldiers being moved into that area. What I would say, also from Jajce, there were a number of Bosnian Croat forces that came down from Jajce as well, so it was not just one-sided.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it correct that then Colonel Blaskic agreed, at or after this meeting you alluded to at the outset of your testimony, to permit the Jajce Brigade from the BH army to pass into the Zenica region?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were there any terms or conditions that were part of that agreement, if you know, with respect to the use, the future use of that brigade by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: Not that I know of. There were a number of terms and conditions regarding the move of the Jajce Brigade in terms of who was going to protect them in case they were attacked en route and the amount of weaponry that they would be able to take with them, but I do not recall any conditions set on them for their future employment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When did they move to Zenica? Can you give us a month?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: I can't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was it before or after the January 1993 conflict in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: It was after the January 1993 conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are you able to tell this Court whether, in fact, the -- was it the 305th Jajce Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: I don't know the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are you able to tell this Court whether that BH army brigade from Jajce, in fact, participated in attacks in the Busovaca municipality, contrary to express agreements between Colonel Blaskic and the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: As I said, I operated in the Gornji Vakuf area until June, and I went through the Lasva Valley maybe twice in six months, so I couldn't give you an answer on that, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your answer is you don't know; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: I don't know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In the January 1993 conflict in Gornji Vakuf, when was the first cease-fire reached?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: There were so many, I'm afraid I lost track. The first real sort of stopping in terms of the -- or the major fighting I think occurred round-about the 26th, maybe the 27th of January. I do not have that information with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let's back up a moment. You said that on January 17th, there was an ultimatum for the BH army to be subordinated to the HVO; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Who made this ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: That ultimatum, as far as I recall, was delivered by the HVO commander in Gornji Vakuf who is Zrinko Tokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was that an ultimatum delivered to Gornji Vakuf or was that an ultimatum made by the HVO throughout the territory of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: Again, I can't answer that definitely, but it was to do with the Vance-Owen Peace Plan and the areas that had been given to the Bosnian Croats under the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, so I would presume, and this is a presumption only, that it is to do with -- it was widespread rather than just to Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What was the expiration date and expiration time of that ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: That evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were there any other similar ultimata that you heard of?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: No, not that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So there was one ultimatum to expire on 17 January, 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: As a liaison officer -- and I'm not looking for any details here -- but is it correct that you reported material information to the milinfocell?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, but as part of the commission, we reported to the joint table, which was Zrinko Tokic, then Colonel Siljeg, and on the other side of the table there was the ARBiH commanders as well, so the information was freely available to all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you have your own milinfocell in Gornji Vakuf, or did the information that you provided as part of that process make its way to the milinfocell in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: We had our own milinfocell in Gornji Vakuf, and I would presume, not working in it, but I would presume that in the normal military chain of command, they would pass their information to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Cheshire Regiment produced one milinfosum per day or were there separate milinfosums produced in Vitez and Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to object, Mr. President. That's beyond the scope of the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Mr. Harmon, please, please. Mr. Hayman, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm just trying to determine, Major, if we were to look for a memorialisation of observations you reported, would we look to the milinfosums that were generated in Vitez or is there some other body of documentation that would be relevant, such as a set of daily milinfosums produced locally in Gornji Vakuf by "B" Company?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: I don't know. I would presume, and this again is a presumption, that the information reported in Gornji Vakuf was included on a "B" Company milinfosum which was then sent to Vitez, and then Vitez would distil the information from the companies and create one milinfosum. So the Vitez one, I presume, would be a distillation of milinfosums from all the companies, and that is normally the way military intelligence operates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said that the fighting actually reduced significantly on the 27th of January?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But that was the first significant lull or reduction in fighting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether there had been, in fact, a cease-fire ordered on the 19th of January by Mate Boban in Gornji Vakuf, some eight days earlier?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: As I said earlier, there were a number of cease-fires, none of which worked, up until the point at which we formed the joint commission and started going round trying to resolve the problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I know you said that, but I'm trying to take the discussion to a higher level of specificity. Do you know whether Mate Boban ordered a cease-fire by the HVO in Gornji Vakuf on 19 January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Defence Exhibit 591, tab 169, could be provided to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Major, this is a document that, if you don't have eye strain, it's almost certain to give you eye strain. I can tell the Court I need new glasses as a result of this case and these beautiful documents provided to us in part by the Office of the Prosecutor. Nonetheless, by what you can make out on this document, it is a milinfosum dated 24 January 1993. Paragraph 1 is titled "Gornji Vakuf," and it appears to talk about Gornji Vakuf. I'm not going to try and read the first paragraph or the outlined information, but I am going to jump down to the bottom of the first page where there's a paragraph that is legible, and I will read it: "A telex was handed in to 'B' Company's location at 1800 hours this evening. It was reported to be a letter from (Commander in Chief) C in C Croatian Defence Council; Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic to Commander HVO Prozor; Colonel Zeljko Siljeg. It stated that the HVO were to stop all offensive operations towards the BiH forces in Gornji Vakuf and that Colonel Siljeg was to obey the orders of President Mate Boban given on the 19th January 1993. Colonel Siljeg was ordered to report to Mostar urgently in order to brief Petkovic on the situation in Gornji Vakuf." Now, my first question is: Were you the only liaison officer attached to "B" Company in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: No, there was Captain Mike Hughes as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this information contained in this milinfosum of 24 January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: I'm not familiar, but now that you've put it in front of me, I do recall something like this happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If, in fact, there was an order for a cease-fire from the supreme commander of the HVO on the 19th of January, 1993, can you share with this Court why it took until the 27th of January, 1993, for even a partial cease-fire to take hold in Gornji Vakuf? Why did it take eight days?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it would be of assistance to turn to another document within this exhibit, tab 22 of Exhibit D591. This is another milinfosum dated 16 January, and if you turn, I would ask the registrar -- the section dealing with Gornji Vakuf begins on page 2 and the relevant paragraph is 2D, which is actually on page 3, so one more page over. Correct. Correct. And it's the large text paragraph. Very good. Thank you. "D. Gornji Vakuf reported that there was still sporadic gunfire and the occasional mortar landing on the town this evening. Last night, Gornji Vakuf came under artillery fire. The resultant craters were believed to be attributed to light artillery shells. Comment: Gornji Vakuf is out of range of light Serb artillery rounds. If B Company's assessment of the craters is correct, then the Croats or the Muslims must have been responsible for last night's shelling. Comment ends. The situation is reported to be worsened by the hard core extremists on both sides who do not appear to be under the control of their respective commanders." Did you report that information to the milinfocell, Major?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: I reported the information concerning the craters which I went and saw, and the information further down on that page I would have reported as well concerning the tank or the self-propelled gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What about the information about the "hard core extremists on both sides who appear to be out of the control of their commanders"; was that information that you reported or that Captain Hughes reported or that someone else reported?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: I would say that that information is an assessment rather than fact that is being reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall that you didn't report it, or what is it that you recall that you can share with this Court?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: I did not report that, and I believe that Captain Hughes did not report that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You think it's wrong?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: If you're asking me for my opinion or what is fact ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, you seem very certain that you didn't report it. Here we are six years later, and I'd like to know why. Why are you certain you didn't report that?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: Because that is an assessment and my job was to report fact on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were there other personnel in "B" Company that made those sorts of assessments and then passed them up to the milinfocell in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: I would presume that that was done by the intelligence personnel or the "B" Company personnel working in the milinfocell.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether these groups, extremist -- "the hard core extremists on both sides," can you further describe that element, either on the HVO side or on the BH army side, for the Court? Was there a name? Was there a unit? Was there a type of dress or uniform?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: No, not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were there HOS in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Speak a little more slowly, please, because the interpreters are running out of breath.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Try to speak a little more slowly. Thank you very much. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: Yes, I saw HOS soldiers, and on a number of the houses that had been burnt in Uzrica and Dusi, there was "HOS" written on the walls with spray paint. Apart from that, I saw no other units which may be regarded as extremists.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How could one differentiate a HOS unit from a non-HOS unit?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: The HOS units I saw were -- some of them were wearing black jackets and they had on their arm a round badge which said "HOS" and "Za Dom Spremni" written on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Major, I know it's been six years, but can you help the Court: Do you know whether General Petkovic and General Pasalic jointly ordered a cease-fire in Gornji Vakuf to take effect on the 20th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: Again, no, I can't recall that. As you said, it was six years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Defence Exhibit 591, tab 24, could be shared with the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This, Major, is a milinfosum from the 22nd of January, 1993, and there appears to be a translation of a document attached to it. Perhaps we could switch the document -- yes. On the back of the first page is, I think, the first page of the attachment. If we move it down a tad -- down a tad, thank you -- we see the heading of the Croatian Defence Council, the main staff of the HVO, and the headquarters of the BH army, a reference number, Mostar, January 20, 1993. "In order that the senseless conflict between Muslims and Croats in Gornji Vakuf can be ended and that we together fight against the Serbo-Chetnik aggression, the headquarters of the HVO and the headquarters of the BH army together issue the following ..." Then there's the text of a command or order. I'll just read a couple of the points: "Simultaneously and without condition all fighting in the region of Gornji Vakuf between the forces of the HVO and the BH army must cease. To bring this about, the following must be completed: "On receipt of orders, all Artillery activity (Guns, Mortar, Tanks) must within two hours cease." And then I jump to paragraph 2: "2. All troops from neighbouring regions be removed from Gornji Vakuf. This must be completed by 1700 hours on January the 21st 1993. "3. To form a commission ..." And so forth. If we then turn, Major, to the last page, I think, of the milinfosum, what we will see is the end of this order. It's typed and has a different appearance. Yes, please. Thank you. We see that this is a document that was or was to be jointly executed by General Petkovic and General Pasalic. Can you tell us, was this, in fact, a cease-fire order that was issued? Was it proposed and discussed? What can you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: I've never seen this document before, so I can't tell you anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, if we could now turn to paragraph 4 of the milinfosum itself which is entitled "Gornji Vakuf"? The first line is not legible. That's why I was hoping you could tell us what this document was so we didn't have to try and pull it out of the milinfosum itself. I see, starting on the third line: "General Morillon and the" something party, something location and "attended the cease-fire talks." If this milinfosum is dated the 22nd of January, were there cease-fire talks in Gornji Vakuf around the 20th or 21st?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: During that period, really, from the 18th onwards, there was an attempt made by UNPROFOR daily to create the conditions for a cease-fire, and I think to help you on that document, it probably says the CO's party, because I believe the commanding officer, Colonel Stewart, came down during that period in an attempt to bring about a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So I take it you have no further recollection of this document which was appended to and was made part of this milinfosum?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court anything other than what you've already provided in terms of the activities that resulted in the burning or destruction of the villages you've described or the units responsible?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: No. As I said, we could -- there was so much fighting going on and we had had one of our soldiers killed and we were not in a position to move out from the base and see what was going on, so we watched from a distance whilst this was happening and then, as soon as we could, and I believe, as I said, after about the 27th, we managed to get round in armoured vehicles to see what was happening. So as to units involved, I can't give you an answer on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said no HVO soldier was disciplined or punished for misconduct that occurred during the conflict in Gornji Vakuf in January. Have you seen the disciplinary records of the HVO in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: No. I said to the best of my knowledge, no HVO soldier or ARBiH soldier was disciplined for any of the things that were reported by the joint commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were there instances of misconduct, indeed crimes or destruction of civilian property, reported on both sides of the warring parties, that is, with respect to both of them?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: At that time, yes, there were. The bulk was obviously against Muslim property, but there were a number of incidents that were investigated that the ARBiH had committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: These two petroleum tankers you described, if they had rolled down the hill where they were, where would they have gone?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: They would have landed in the Muslim section of Gornji Vakuf or the part of the town that was being held by the ARBiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was the fighting in Gornji Vakuf going on right in the middle of the town; in other words, was the town split into two parts with the front line down the middle, in essence?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: That's a very simplistic view, but it was, yes, effectively split in half.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: These 20 soldiers that you saw south of Gornji Vakuf with HV patches, what did you see them doing? What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: At the time, they were standing or milling around the checkpoint area at Karamustafic. As I said, I was on a patrol in two armoured vehicles and we were stopped there waiting to pick up a convoy to bring them back, to bring the convoy back through Gornji Vakuf, and they were just standing around at the area of the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you see them do anything other than milling around?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harmon, do you have any additional questions to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: A question from Judge Rodrigues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Major, I'm going to ask you only one question: How do you distinguish between the HVO soldiers and the HV soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NICHOLAS SHORT
utterances.text: Sir, the HV soldiers have a different badge on their arm with just HV rather than HVO, and that's what the soldiers were wearing, a large shield-type badge with HV and the checkerboard underneath. I think it was underneath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. I don't have any further questions to ask you. We have finished. You can go back to your unit now. The registrar will accompany the witness out of the courtroom, and we can move on with the rest of our work this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. This is part of the rebuttal. Mr. Harmon, do you have any other witnesses? Does this mean that you're not going to have any other witness throughout your rebuttal? This is a question which is of interest to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have one, possibly two more witnesses, Mr. President. They will be brief witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. But according to what Mr. Fourmy said, not before the week beginning the 6th of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: 5th of July, I believe, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me move to introduce Prosecutor's Exhibit 747 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No comments? All right. It's been tendered. 747 is listed as an exhibit for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have some additional documents we would like to present to the Chamber, Mr. President. Some will have to be presented in closed session. I will reserve those till the end of this afternoon or the end of this session, and I have then two small items we're prepared to present to the Chamber today. Let me begin, first of all, Mr. President, with a single exhibit. I, first of all, would direct Your Honours' attention to the testimony of Colonel Blaskic found at page 18062 and found at lines 1 through 4, as well as the same page, lines 9 through 12, and in his testimony, Colonel Blaskic said, and I quote: "From the 8th of November onwards, I was responsible to Mr. Prkacin who, at that particular time, was the commander of the Central Bosnian Operation Zone." Further in his answer, he says: "In November, Prkacin commanded the entire area of the Central Bosnia Operation Zone, and at that first meeting held on the 8th of November, the commanders of the municipal staff refused to comply." We would submit -- Mr. President, we have submitted other documents showing that Colonel Blaskic was the Operative Zone commander at that time, but we would offer now into evidence this particular document, which I will just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is this being contested? Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I don't know what exactly counsel is responding to. There was a joint command, Colonel Blaskic was the Operative Zone commander; then there was a joint command over the territory. I don't know what this document is, so I can't say, Mr. President, whether this is extraneous or not in terms of the Defence's position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can be perfectly clear on this, Mr. President. The state of the record and the state of the testimony of Colonel Blaskic was, from the 8th of November onwards: "I was responsible for Mr. Prkacin, and Prkacin, at that particular time, was the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone." That is the state of the record, and we are offering this document and we have offered other documents to show that in November, Colonel Blaskic was the commander of the Central Bosnia Operation Zone, and this particular exhibit indicates, at the end of the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let's not spend too much time with that. You simply can file it and we will note it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document 748.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I hope that after two years of trial, we're not going to begin challenging the situation of the head of the Operative Zone in Central Bosnia, which was Colonel Blaskic. That would be very worrying.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, it was just a question of clarifying the record, and that's the state of the record that we have found in part, and we want to clarify the record, and we submit this as evidence in respect of that testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I hope that you're not going to ask us to clarify every line of the 30.000 pages of transcript, Mr. Harmon. Very well. What is the exhibit number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 748.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. It's been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, what I propose to do is just select certain areas of the transcript and where there has been testimony on particular points and submit to Your Honours evidence of rebuttal in respect of that. If I could direct your attention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Very well. Starting with the accused's testimony or testimony of other people as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It would be other people's testimony as well, and it's not in any particular sequence, Mr. President, or by category --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, do you have an objection? I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No objection to the presentation of documents, Mr. President, but we do object to a miniature argument with respect to each document, because if counsel's going to frame why this is relevant and this is what it is and this is what you should conclude, that's not a rebuttal case, that's closing argument. The Court knows, we presented three volumes of documents and we didn't argue to the Court. We gave you the documents. This is his turn to give the Court additional documents and then both sides can argue the case at the end of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I very much appreciate your procedural lesson, but I think that you're really obsessed with your own procedures. I come from a system where, as you know, things don't work that way, but I accept the proceedings that we use here, that the Judges have adopted themselves. This is part of the rebuttal, and I think during rebuttal, it is permissible for the Prosecutor to choose things, he can present witnesses, present testimony, bring in documents, and can decide that in respect of this or that point in the transcript or this or that testimony, he wants to argue something, and perhaps you, during your surrebuttal, you can answer. We don't have to say anything further than that. Would you like to surrebut further, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can we comment on his rebuttal documents in our surrebuttal, just counsel comment on the document? Because we'd like to, if that's acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You can do what you like during your surrebuttal. I see no problem with that. But not now. Now let the Prosecutor do his work, his rebuttal right. Mr. Harmon? I do like to consult with my colleagues here so that we work together. I'm going to ask if I've made a mistake, because I'm not always familiar with the customs that you use procedurally, that is, between Mr. Harmon and yourself, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I can never thank my wise colleagues enough. I think that the Prosecutor can present exhibits and can make a short comment, not a long one, and without arguments. Arguments are reserved for July. Do you agree with that position, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does it comply with your own customs, your own procedures? And I would like to thank my colleagues, as I always do. Mr. Harmon, please continue. All right. You are answering an argument or a passage? Explain what it is. Say the passage that you are talking about and move on to the next one. Thank you very much. We will take a break in ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm thanking the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The next item is -- the next items are four exhibits. They relate to testimony that is found on pages 13889 through 13892, and they relate to Defence Exhibit 412. Exhibit 412 is a document which indicates the date of death of a particular individual whose name is Nedjeljko Grabovac. These and the Defence Exhibit indicates that this individual died on the 16th of April, 1993. I tender to Your Honours four exhibits which indicate that this individual died on the 22nd of December, 1993, as is indicated in an exhibit that was also tendered by the Defence, that is, Exhibit 345. I don't want to belabour the point, Mr. President. When you read the transcript and Your Honours read the transcript, it will become apparent precisely why these exhibits are being entered into evidence. These are documents, Mr. President, that were seized pursuant to a search warrant executed by the -- a search warrant that was executed by the Office of the Prosecutor and authorised by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Are you going to give it a number, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're waiting, I have two other sets of documents that need to be presented but they should be presented in closed session. Mr. Dubuisson, if you could identify which exhibit number -- tell me, since I've given you four, by referring to the ERN number on the upper right-hand side of the document, it would assist me in marking my exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: All right. The document which ends in 663 is document 749. The document ending 664 is document 750. The one which ends in 667 is 751. The one that ends with 668 is document 752.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I suggest that we take a break now, Mr. Harmon. That will allow the public gallery to realise that right after you're going to make a different presentation. Are you going to take a long time to present the documents? Will the closed session go on for a long time? I'd like to say this for the public gallery.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It will last about 15 minutes and then we have no additional evidence to present today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. All right. We're going to adjourn the hearing for about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 4.38 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 25th day of June, 1999, at 9.00 a.m.
